title: Trump says reported FBI database hack is ‘not good’
rawText:
The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to reports in CNN and the Associated Press.
The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more. The scope of the breach does not yet appear to be clear.
A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”
President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”
In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack.

title: 'Officials can't use common sense' - was Rogers handball correct?
rawText:
'Officials can't use common sense' - was Rogers handball correct?
- Published
It is rare when a key handball decision is given for the widespread response to be "that is correct".
Often the discussion centres on the desire for a seemingly more lenient interpretation taking into account perceived intent.
And that is again a talking point after the crucial penalty given against Chelsea in Saturday's 4-1 home defeat by Leeds which ended up putting the visitors ahead for the first time.
Interestingly, despite the perception, handball penalties are much rarer in the Premier League compared with the other top five leagues in Europe.
Last season, there were 22 penalties for handball in the English top flight's 380 games - easily the lowest tally.
Spain's La Liga (36) and Italy's Serie A (38) produced the most.
This season in the Premier League there have been three in 106 matches - less than in 2025-26.
So why was the penalty given against Chelsea's Morgan Rogers?
- 'Fragile' and 'miles off it' - Alonso's Chelsea honeymoon is over 
  - Published8 minutes ago
Why the penalty was given
The feeling among Premier League clubs is that handball is in a good place now, where the arm must either be fully extended away from the body, raised, or be a deliberate act to be punishable.
And it is the last of these that applied to the penalty given against Rogers, which to some might seem a bit harsh, considering the Premier League's more relaxed interpretation of handball.
There are, however, a few key reasons why referee Michael Oliver pointed to the spot, why the video assistant referee (VAR) did not intervene, and why it will be judged as a correct decision.
Two of the factors which a referee looks for when judging a potential handball apply here.
First, how far the ball travelled.
As Jayden Bogle's shot was from distance, a defender is considered to have more time to adjust their body and react - and thus avoid a potential handball.
Most important in this case is the movement of the arm.
When Bogle shoots, Rogers' arm is not raised - but it comes up to the flight of the ball.
Crucially, had Rogers kept his arm in its original position - lower and level with his midriff - there would not have been a handball offence.
What does this mean? Put simply, if the ball would have hit the body if it had not come off the arm, it is considered to have no impact.
But this case was different. Rogers raised his arm and that is what led to the ball being deflected away. This is considered a deliberate act, and this trumps all other considerations.
Was there any case not to give it?
Perhaps there was a question about whether the ball hit Rogers too high on his arm, and thus should not be a handball offence.
It was close, but it looked like it was in what the laws call the 'red zone', the part of the arm which is punishable for handball.
But this really would be the only reason the VAR, Michael Salisbury, would have any cause to consider an on-field review.
We saw a similar case last season, in terms of how this kind of handball offence is judged - coincidentally involving a penalty awarded to Leeds.
As Anton Stach's powerful strike arrowed towards goal, Everton defender James Tarkowski leaned to his left in an attempt to block the shot - and did so with his arm, which was tucked tightly to the side of his body.
Everton manager David Moyes described the decision as "wrong", but it was absolutely correct in law.
That Tarkowski's arm was close to his side was irrelevant because of the deliberate act of leaning into the path of the ball.
Likewise, Rogers raised his arm to stop the ball and a penalty was a justifiable call.
Decision underlines dissatisfaction with handball law
Despite the Premier League having a more lenient interpretation of the handball law already, it is clear that many observers would like it to go further.
For example, BBC Match of the Day pundit Alan Shearer echoed many when he said there should be more intent for a handball.

title: The FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked
rawText:
Friday, it was reported that both the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the FBI were hacked. In reporting on the FBI hack, CNN noted that this is the second such attack on the agency in the last few months, this time targeting the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which federal, state, and local law enforcement use to share information, including warrants and missing persons. President Donald Trump later confirmed the hack in an interview with Fox News. NBC first reported the USDA hack on Friday. According to Reuters:
The FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked
The list of hacks hitting the US government over the last few months keeps growing.
While the payments database is the known extent of the intrusion so far, the former officials warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety data and research on animal-borne illnesses, according to the report.
The breaches come following a week of major outages across several sectors, including at the FAA and NSA, which the government has sought to reassure the public were not the result of a cyberattack.
President Trump suggested that the breach of the FBI might not be an entirely bad thing, telling Fox News that, “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” and “wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?” referring to investigations into his ties to Russia.
The FBI suffered a breach, reported in late September, that allegedly compromised personal records of “all FBI employees and applicants.” This was followed by a hack of DHS, reported in October, comprising 40,000 employee records. In the wake of these major outages, the White House national cyber director, Sean Cairncross, stepped down this week.
Update November 21st: Added President Trump’s comments.

title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
rawText:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy
Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.
It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.
Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.
There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”
The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.
Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.
Caddy
Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.
For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.
Comma
Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.
Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.
It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.
Comma is free to start and open source.
Fambot
Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.
The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. title: Superb England run up record win over New Zealand
rawText:
Superb England run up record win over New Zealand
- Published
England (19) 37
Tries: Slade, Van Poortvliet, Earl, Chessum, Atkinson Cons: F Smith (2), M Smith Pens: M Smith (2)
New Zealand (5) 12
Tries: De Groot, B Barrett Cons: McKenzie
England's revival roared up a gear as they beat New Zealand by a record margin after former captain Lewis Moody led the hosts' response to the haka.
Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease last year, stood at the centre of a flying V formation that England had adopted for their victories over the same opponents last year and in the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final.
In terms of margin, this win trumped both - and the other seven England victories in the teams' 121-year rivalry.
And the hosts were full value for it. They dominated the All Blacks from the start.
Henry Slade crossed for the opening try in the fourth minute and only England's own mistakes prevented them taking a bigger lead than their 19-5 advantage into the break.
Beauden Barrett marked his 150th Test appearance by rounding off a coast-to-coast Kiwi try to cut England's advantage to 24-12. But his team never really threatened to reel in Steve Borthwick's men.
England introduced five forwards off the bench in the immediate aftermath of that 55th-minute score and, with Ellis Genge in fearsome carrying form, they had more than enough to see out victory in comfort.
Seb Atkinson took a delayed pop pass from Marcus Smith to stroll in for England's fifth try just after the hour.
The hosts finished the game camped down in the New Zealand 22m in search of a sixth score while choruses of Swing Low rolled around the stands.
For New Zealand, who suffered a shock defeat by Wales last weekend, it is a result that suggests a long Test season, which included four Tests against South Africa, may be catching up with them.
By contrast England, who could still end up in next weekend's Nations Championship grand final depending on results, are riding a wave of confidence.
- Ex-captain Moody joins England in emotional haka response 
  - Published2 hours ago
Moody sets the mood
Moody's involvement in the pre-match challenge ensured New Zealand were met by a wall of noise and relentless pressure from kick-off.
Fast starts have become a feature of England's autumn campaign so far, with Australia and Japan both blitzed in the opening minutes.
New Zealand are a class above those teams, but fared little better against the revved-up hosts.
The game was only four minutes old when Slade, with roars from the stands at his back, won the race to a Fin Smith grubber.
After that initial strike, England maintained a stranglehold on the match.
A brilliant 50:22 from George Furbank bought more territory and England, hitting hard in defence, penned New Zealand back.
Their dominance did not immediately translate into points.
Individual errors - Jack van Poortvliet's fumble at the back of a breakdown, Fin Smith's over-cooked cross-field kick, Alex Coles being held up over the line - meant chances went begging.
After half an hour, England had enjoyed 74% of possession, 82% of territory and made 183 metres to New Zealand's 34. A sense the hosts may ultimately regret those mistakes nagged at fans in the stands.
It proved misplaced. Van Poortvliet plunged over from short range after a Cadan Murley break and then, four minutes later, the excellent Ben Earl thundered off the back of a scrum, trampled through Cam Roigard and went under the posts.
New Zealand prop Ethan de Groot burrowed over to repair some of the damage, but at 19-5 down at the break, the visitors were both reeling and somewhat fortunate to still be in touch.
England started the second half at the same breathless pace that marked their approach to the first. Ollie Chessum, lurking out wide, ploughed through the unfortunate Will Jordan for a try inside two minutes of the restart.

title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
rawText:
AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
- Date:
- November 21, 2026
- Source:
- York University
- Summary:
- AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.
For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI
The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.
If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.
"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.
Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.
AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
rawText:
Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
- Date:
- November 21, 2026
- Source:
- Kyushu University
- Summary:
- Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.
- Share:
We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.
Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.
Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time
Now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times."
Atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.
Modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.
A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times
The researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.
"It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times."
That improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

title: Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
rawText:
A bullet-peppered mural of the Haitian striker Emmanuel Sanon covers the facade of Port-au-Prince’s main football ground. But more than two years have passed since any sports stars graced the pitch.
In 2024, as the surrounding city was almost entirely captured by heavily armed gangs, Sylvio Cator stadium – where football greats including Brazil’s Ronaldo and Roberto Carlos once played – also fell under criminal control, its dilapidated red and blue stands used as an outpost by fighters working for a gang boss called Izo. Haiti’s national team, the Grenadiers, found itself homeless and was forced to play its World Cup qualifying games abroad.
That changed last week, as Haitian police and troops from El Salvador reconquered the stadium. Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, called the development a step towards delivering Haiti from a criminal insurrection that has displaced more than 1.5 million people and killed thousands.
“We now have the upper hand on the ground,” claimed Bukele, who has sent more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti since mid-October.
Outside the Sylvio Cator stadium, named after an acclaimed Haitian athlete who won a silver medal at the 1928 Olympics, there were joyous scenes as citizens celebrated a foreign politician they hope will prove an unlikely saviour.
“There’s a wind of hope blowing through our country and, thanks to God, we will get through this. Long live Bukele!” said a 55-year-old decorator who asked to be named as Bòs Baton.
Stood by Sanon’s battle-scarred fresco, Baton recalled being driven from an area called Poste-Marchand after criminals set his home ablaze during an armed uprising that started in February 2024. “Today, we are happy because there are places we couldn’t go to before that are accessible – and it’s thanks to Bukele’s intervention that we can be here today,” Baton said.
Identical sentiments have been voiced on the streets of El Salvador’s capital, San Salvador, in recent years as a result of Bukele’s controversial anti-gang crusade, which has freed millions from gang rule – albeit at a high price.
Since that crackdown began in early 2022, more than 90,000 Salvadorans have been jailed as part of a mass incarceration campaign that has slashed murder rates but also fuelled fears that El Salvador’s democracy has died.
Bukele’s domestic clampdown has made the millennial strongman a darling for rightwing politicians and voters across Latin America and the Caribbean, who hold his actions up as proof that, with an iron fist and a malleable approach to human rights, rampant criminality can be tamed.
Now, as Bukele seeks to extend his seven-year presidency in an election in February, he is hoping to burnish his gang-busting credentials overseas.
“It’s an operation that projects force, that projects Bukele’s image as the saviour … and positions El Salvador as a key reference in the region for [how] … to deal with gangs and security,” said Tiziano Breda, a Latin America regional expert from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project.
The extent of Bukele’s ambitions in Haiti is unclear. The operation’s trigger was the 18 October abduction of four Salvadoran aviation technicians who worked for a UN-backed security force. On Monday, Bukele’s vice-president, Félix Ulloa, announced Salvadoran troops would withdraw as soon as the four men were rescued, “because this is not an occupying force – we are not there to stay”.
But Ulloa also said his government was responding altruistically “to a cry for help from the Haitian people and government”, suggesting its mission could be extended.
Bukele has also hinted his plans go beyond short-lived ground operations to recover his citizens, or their remains. “We will triumph. God will give us victory,” the politician vowed this week.
Many Haitians hope his combatants will stay and have been thrilled by cinematic social media clips posted by Bukele showing helicopter strikes on a gang compound and the mansion of a gangster nicknamed Taliba

title: Rockstar says GTA VI made $3.79 billion in its first day
rawText:
GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day of sales, which set “a new record for entertainment across any medium,” according to an announcement from Rockstar Games. The game also sold 32.5 million in pre-orders.
Rockstar says GTA VI made $3.79 billion in its first day
GTA VI is finally here, and it’s already a huge hit.
“It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder. said in a statement “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.” Rockstar claims that the game’s release, which happened Thursday, was “the biggest entertainment launch in history.”
The news follows leaks, delays, and a huge amount of interest ahead of GTA VI’s launch. (Many other games steered clear of GTA VI to get their time in the sun.) But even with the weight of anticipation placed upon GTA VI, it actually lived up to the hype, my colleague Andrew Webster said in his review.

title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous’ penalties on companies that build data centers overseas
rawText:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he plans to restrict U.S. companies from building data centers overseas — the latest instance of the president embracing the construction of massive tech facilities that a majority of Americans oppose.
Back in Washington after a trip to Asia, Trump said the restrictions were necessary to prevent AI infrastructure from leaving U.S. shores.
“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump told reporters in the White House briefing room.
“We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country,” he said.
He added that the U.S. would tax any company that attempted to build a data center abroad.
“We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” he said.
The comments signaled a potential new headache for the artificial intelligence industry, on a day when stock markets tumbled and not even the record-setting IPO this week of Anthropic could soothe investors’ fears about the sustainability of AI stocks.
They were also the latest example of Trump’s forceful advocacy for AI data centers, a position that puts him squarely at odds with the majority of Americans.
“You ought to take advantage of the data centers,” Trump said Friday. “Make them pay you. Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don’t shut them off.”
Trump has previously attacked state and local efforts to roll back data center construction, saying in August that they should only be stopped if communities “want to end up being backwards and poor.”
“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” Trump wrote in a social media post.
During this year’s midterm elections, data centers proved a key sticking point for voters, who overwhelmingly supported candidates who promised to curb their proliferation.
On Wall Street, the massive wins by Democrats who pledged to rein in data centers put a fresh dent in an already-ailing AI stock trade, as investors digested the prospect that tech companies’ computing resources would be further crimped.
Since Nov. 4, the S&P 500 has declined approximately 9%, though a confluence of other factors has also contributed to the brutal sell-off.
It is not clear how Trump’s foreign data center ban would be implemented; a White House representative did not immediately reply to a request for comment Friday.
Trump admitted that he had not yet told his staff about the plan.
“I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump mused. “I’m telling them now — they’re here, many of them are here — and we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can’t. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them if they do it.”

title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
rawText:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.
“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.
He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.
In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.
Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.
“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

title: Hegseth alardea de la captura de Maduro en la primera visita a Venezuela de un secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. en décadas
rawText:
Hegseth alardea de la captura de Maduro en la primera visita a Venezuela de un secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. en décadas
  - Autor, Redacción
  - Título del autor, BBC News Mundo
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 3 min
"Hoy hace exactamente un año, el imputado fugitivo narcoterrorista Nicolás Maduro, el hombre que pasó más de una década entregándoles las fronteras y el territorio de Venezuela a terroristas de todas partes del mundo, se paró en un escenario no muy lejos de aquí y gritó en tono de burla: 'Vengan y agárrenme'. Bueno, nosotros respondimos a ese llamado".
Con esas palabras, el secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. Pete Hegseth, presumió de la captura de Maduro durante una visita a Venezuela en la que se reunió con la presidenta interina, Delcy Rodríguez, para firmar un acuerdo de cooperación militar.
Durante un discurso pronunciado en la sede de la Embajada de EE.UU. Hegseth describió la captura de Maduro como "la operación militar más sofisticada en la historia de América Latina" y aseguró que el 3 de enero -cuando fue ejecutada- pasará a la historia de Venezuela como "un día de liberación".
"Es un gran honor ser el primer secretario de Guerra en este siglo en pisar Venezuela. El peso de este momento no se me escapa. Hace apenas un año, mi presencia aquí, nuestra presencia aquí habría sido considerada imposible, casi inimaginable", dijo.
Hegseth afirmó que eso había sido posible gracias al mandatario estadounidense, Donald Trump.
"Tuvo el coraje para hacer lo que ningún presidente anterior estuvo dispuesto a hacer: defender la patria estadounidense con acciones, no solo con palabras. Y porque él lo hizo hace casi un año, los mejores y más valientes guerreros estadounidenses solucionaron un problema de 27 años de antigüedad para este hemisferio en cuestión de horas", apuntó.
"El resultado fue, como había predicho Maduro, 'no guerra, sí paz'. Paz a través de la fuerza para llevar a narcoterroristas hasta la justicia y empezar un nuevo capítulo para EE.UU., para Venezuela, para los militares venezolanos y para el hemisferio occidental", agregó luego.
Cooperación militar
La visita del jefe del Pentágono a Caracas se produjo en el contexto de una gira por países de América Latina.
Antes de su discurso en la sede diplomática, Hegseth acudió al Palacio de Miraflores, sede del Poder Ejecutivo, donde firmó con Delcy Rodríguez un acuerdo de cooperación militar entre el Pentágono y las Fuerzas Armadas de Venezuela.
El alto funcionario estadounidense dijo que se trata del "restablecimiento" de lazos militares entre ambos países.
Aunque no se ofrecieron muchos detalles, la prensa oficial en Venezuela aseguró que se trata de un acuerdo que "respetará la independencia y la soberanía nacional".
Hegseth calificó el pacto como "un restablecimiento de nuestra alianza de defensa" y afirmó que traía los saludos del presidente Trump, quien esperaba con interés trabajar juntos. "No solo en el ámbito militar contra los narcoterroristas y las organizaciones criminales", dijo, "sino también en el económico, aprovechando las extraordinarias capacidades de recursos de Venezuela".
Por su parte, Delcy Rodríguez elogió lo que describió como la "madurez política" que había permitido a estos dos antiguos enemigos reconstruir sus relaciones de trabajo. El acuerdo con el Pentágono "fortalecerá la capacidad de la Fuerza Armada Nacional Bolivariana", afirmó, al proporcionar "equipamiento operativo" y acceso a nuevas tecnologías.
El objetivo de este último acuerdo firmado con Washington, añadió, es "hacer frente a amenazas comunes".
Desde la captura de Maduro en enero, Estados Unidos asumió una suerte de tutela sobre Venezuela que incluye el control sobre la venta del petróleo de ese país. Además, respaldó la permanencia de Delcy Rodríguez en el poder como presidenta interina.

title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
rawText:
A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.
Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.
Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
rawText:
Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.
Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela. Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.
“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.
In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.
“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.
Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.
“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.
During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.
But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”
Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.
Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.

title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
rawText:
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.
Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.
The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.
Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.
In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.
If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).
According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.
In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.
“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.
The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

title: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
rawText:
NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
- Date:
- November 17, 2026
- Source:
- NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
- Summary:
- NASA has successfully tested Mars helicopter rotor blades at supersonic speeds, boosting potential lift by 30% and overcoming a major obstacle to more powerful aircraft on the Red Planet. The breakthrough could enable next-generation helicopters to carry heavier scientific equipment, fly farther, and explore places beyond the reach of traditional rovers.
- Share:
NASA is pushing the limits of helicopter flight on Mars, testing rotor blades at speeds once considered too risky. The faster these blades spin, the more lift they can generate, potentially allowing future aircraft to carry heavier scientific instruments and travel greater distances across the Red Planet.
During tests conducted in March at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, engineers successfully pushed the tips of experimental Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound without causing them to break apart. The experiments took place inside a specialized chamber designed to reproduce the harsh atmospheric conditions on Mars. Results from 137 test runs could help engineers develop a new generation of more powerful aircraft capable of carrying scientific equipment.
"NASA had a great run with the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, but we are asking these next-generation aircraft to do even more at the Red Planet," said Al Chen, Mars Exploration Program manager at JPL. "That's not an easy ask. While everything about Mars is hard, flying there is just about the hardest thing you can do. That's because its atmosphere is so incredibly thin that it is hard to generate lift, and yet Mars has significant gravity."
Ingenuity made history on April 19, 2021, when it became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another world. However, it was designed primarily to demonstrate that flight on Mars was possible, not to transport scientific instruments. NASA now hopes to go much further. Its recently announced SkyFall project, along with other potential future aircraft, could carry sensors and scientific instruments to investigate Mars from the air. Flying at low altitudes would provide valuable information to support future robotic and human missions.
Why Flying on Mars Requires Extreme Rotor Speeds
Helicopters generate more thrust by spinning their rotors faster or using blades with a larger diameter. That basic principle applies on Earth and Mars, but the Red Planet presents a much greater engineering challenge.
Mars has an atmosphere only about 1% as dense as Earth's, leaving helicopter blades with far fewer air molecules to push against. To produce enough lift, engineers must operate rotors at exceptionally high speeds, bringing their tips close to the speed of sound. Small rotors on Earth can also spin thousands of times per minute, but the denser atmosphere makes it unnecessary to push their tips toward supersonic speeds to generate substantial lift.
During Ingenuity's 72 flights on Mars, its engineers limited the helicopter's composite-skinned foam rotors to 2,700 revolutions per minute. This restriction served two important purposes. It kept the blades away from the complex and potentially unpredictable conditions near the sound barrier, and it provided a safety margin in case sudden winds (from a dust devil, for instance) caused the blade tips to move faster relative to the surrounding air.
"If Chuck Yeager were here, he'd tell you things can get squirrely around Mach 1," said JPL's Jaakko Karras, the rotor test lead. "With that in mind, we planned Ingenuity's flights to keep the rotor blade tips at Mach 0.7 with no wind so that if we encountered a Martian headwind while in flight, the rotor tips wouldn't go supersonic. But we want more performance from our next-gen Mars aircraft. We needed to know that our rotors could go faster safely."

title: Cómo fue el sofisticado ataque con el que Ucrania destruyó parte del preciado puente de Crimea de Putin (y qué consecuencias tendrá)
rawText:
Cómo fue el sofisticado ataque con el que Ucrania destruyó parte del preciado puente de Crimea de Putin (y qué consecuencias tendrá)
  - Autor, Laura Gozzi
  - Título del autor, BBC News
  - Autor, Ilya Abishev
  - Título del autor, Corresponsal de Defensa de BBC en Rusia
  - Autor, Richard Irvine-Brown
  - Título del autor, BBC Verify
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 6 min
El puente de Crimea, que atraviesa el estrecho de Kerch sobre el mar Negro, ha sido un símbolo desde que se acabó su construcción.
Para Rusia, es un proyecto prestigioso que consolida su reivindicación sobre el territorio ucraniano soberano. Para Ucrania, una infraestructura detestada, emblemática de la ocupación de la península de Crimea por parte de Moscú.
Una sección clave del puente de doble arco y 19 kilómetros de longitud yace ahora en el fondo del mar, derribada por el armamento ucraniano de largo alcance en una operación de siete fases que culminó en un dramático derrumbe.
El portavoz del Kremlin, Dmitri Peskov, ha declarado que el puente "será reconstruido y quedará incluso mejor que antes".
Pero ocho años después de su inauguración, el puente se ha convertido en una prueba material de la capacidad de Kyiv para atravesar las defensas militares de Moscú y alcanzar incluso sus estructuras más preciadas y protegidas.
Una operación en 7 etapas
El ataque contra el estratégico puente de Crimea se llevó a cabo de forma gradual para atravesar distintas capas de defensa, según informó Kyiv este martes.
Durante varias semanas, el Servicio de Seguridad de Ucrania y su Estado Mayor destruyeron gradualmente sistemas de defensa aérea, radares, sistemas de guerra electrónica y otros objetivos designados, dijo el presidente Volodymyr Zelensky.
El 16 de noviembre ya se había registrado un incidente importante cuando varios drones impactaron el puente durante la noche. El tráfico se interrumpió y luego se reanudó. Aunque el arco que se alza sobre la calzada resultó visiblemente dañado, la estructura no colapsó.
Pero ese golpe resultó ser solo la penúltima etapa de un ataque complejo.
En la madrugada del 17 de noviembre, los ataques finales dieron el golpe definitivo a la ya debilitada estructura del arco.
Un vídeo verificado –grabado desde una cámara a bordo de un misil Flamingo de fabricación ucraniana– muestra al arma acercándose al tramo principal del puente y dirigiéndose hacia los arcos de acero, con la grabación congelándose justo antes del impacto.
Según Justin Bronk, experto en municiones del Royal United Services Institute, el misil Flamingo podría haber sido modificado para ser controlado a la distancia, lo que mejoró su precisión lo suficiente como para alcanzar los pilares del puente.
Bronk añadió que la "ojiva muy pesada" del misil lo hacía "más adecuado" para atacar los tramos y soportes de hormigón armado del puente.
Más tarde, Zelensky confirmó que en el ataque se utilizaron varios tipos de misiles y drones, lo que llevó al colapso del enorme arco, una estructura de unos 227 metros de longitud y un peso de miles de toneladas.
Las imágenes diurnas captadas desde la costa norte de Crimea muestran que un tramo de aproximadamente 200 metros de la carretera se desplomó y fue arrastrado al mar
Se trata claramente de un daño crítico para el puente. Lejos de ser un mero elemento decorativo, el arco desempeñaba una función estructural. Distribuía las cargas, sostenía el tramo principal y contribuía a garantizar la estabilidad de toda la estructura.
El arco paralelo que sostiene el tramo ferroviario se ha mantenido en pie, aunque es posible que también haya sufrido daños. En un primer momento, se suspendió todo el tráfico en el puente, aunque después permitieron que los trenes reanudaran su circulación.
Sin embargo, los daños en el tramo principal del puente son "catastróficos", declaró a BBC Verify Colin Capriani, ingeniero estructural de la Universidad de Monash en Melbourne, Australia.
